tips.title: CoroutineContext elements combine via the + operator
tips.content:
A CoroutineContext is a set of elements (Job, Dispatcher, exception
handler, name) combined with +. Adding two contexts merges their elements,
with the right-hand side overriding any element of the same key already
present on the left.

This is how launch(Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("sync")) composes a
custom dispatcher and a debug name into a single context passed to the new
coroutine, without needing a builder object.

tips.title: Choosing Dispatchers.IO, Default, or Unconfined has real performance implications
tips.content:
Dispatchers.IO is backed by a large, elastic thread pool tuned for blocking
calls (network, disk); Dispatchers.Default is a fixed pool sized to CPU
cores, meant for CPU-bound work like sorting or parsing large data.

Using Default for blocking I/O starves the small CPU pool and can stall
unrelated CPU work app-wide; using IO for CPU-bound work wastes its
elastic-thread design. Dispatchers.Unconfined resumes on whatever thread
triggered the suspension — it exists mainly for testing, not production
code paths.
tips.codeSnippet:
suspend fun readFile() = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { file.readText() }
suspend fun parseJson(raw: String) = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { Json.decode(raw) }

tips.title: Rethrow CancellationException instead of swallowing it in catch blocks
tips.content:
A broad `catch (e: Exception)` also catches CancellationException, since
it's a subtype of Exception — swallowing it silently breaks structured
concurrency, because the coroutine appears to keep running instead of
honoring its cancellation.

Always check for CancellationException first and rethrow it, or catch a
more specific exception type instead of the broad Exception supertype.

tips.title: NonCancellable context lets cleanup code survive a cancelled coroutine
tips.content:
Once a coroutine is cancelled, any suspend call inside it (including in a
finally block) throws CancellationException immediately — so an await on
a cleanup network call inside finally would just fail instead of running.

withContext(NonCancellable) { ... } creates a scope that ignores the
surrounding cancellation, letting genuinely necessary cleanup (releasing a
lock, closing a resource over the network) complete even after the parent
coroutine has been cancelled.

tips.title: CoroutineExceptionHandler only fires on uncaught exceptions in root coroutines
tips.content:
A CoroutineExceptionHandler installed on a child coroutine's context is
ignored — exceptions propagate up to the nearest root coroutine (one
launched directly on a scope, not a child of another coroutine) before the
handler is consulted.

It also doesn't work with async — exceptions from async are stored in the
resulting Deferred and only surface when you call .await(), bypassing the
handler entirely. Install the handler on the top-level scope, not on
individual launch calls.

tips.title: yield() cooperatively checks for cancellation inside tight CPU-bound loops
tips.content:
A pure computation loop with no suspend calls inside it never checks
whether its coroutine has been cancelled, so cancel() has no effect until
the loop finishes on its own.

Calling yield() periodically inside the loop gives the coroutine a chance
to check for cancellation and throw if it's been cancelled, while also
letting other coroutines run on the same dispatcher in the meantime.

tips.title: Mutex is the coroutine-safe replacement for synchronized blocks
tips.content:
Java's synchronized keyword blocks the underlying thread, which is
dangerous inside a suspend function — it can hold a thread hostage across
a suspension point, or deadlock a limited dispatcher thread pool entirely.

kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex provides withLock {} as a suspend-aware
equivalent — it suspends the coroutine instead of blocking the thread
while waiting for the lock, making it safe to use around suspend calls.

tips.title: Cancelling a parent Job cancels every child, but not the other way around
tips.content:
Structured concurrency's parent-child Job hierarchy means calling
cancel() on a parent scope propagates down to every coroutine launched
within it — but a child coroutine failing (for non-CancellationException
reasons) propagates its exception up and cancels its siblings too, unless
the parent uses a SupervisorJob.

Understanding this hierarchy is essential for reasoning about lifecycle-
bound scopes like viewModelScope — cancelling the ViewModel's scope
reliably cancels every coroutine it launched, directly or nested.
tips.codeSnippet:
val parentJob = Job()
val scope = CoroutineScope(parentJob)

scope.launch { launch { delay(5000) } } // nested child
parentJob.cancel() // cancels the outer launch AND its nested child

tips.title: withContext switches dispatchers without spawning a new coroutine
tips.content:
It's tempting to think withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { ... } launches a new
concurrent coroutine, but it doesn't — it suspends the current coroutine,
switches its execution to the new dispatcher, runs the block, and resumes
the original coroutine on the original dispatcher afterward.

This makes withContext sequential, not concurrent — for actual
concurrency, you still need async/launch inside it. withContext is purely
for moving where a piece of sequential logic executes.

tips.title: ensureActive() is a lighter-weight cancellation check than yield()
tips.content:
yield() both checks for cancellation and gives up the thread so other
coroutines can run — but that thread-yielding has overhead you don't
always need, especially in a loop where you just want to fail fast on
cancellation without ceding execution.

ensureActive() only throws if the coroutine has been cancelled; it doesn't
suspend or yield the thread, making it cheaper for hot loops that only
need cancellation responsiveness, not cooperative multitasking.

tips.title: launch starts fire-and-forget work; async returns an awaitable result
tips.content:
launch returns a Job and is for coroutines you don't need a result from —
sending an analytics event, for example. If it throws, the exception
propagates immediately to the parent scope.

async returns a Deferred<T>, meant for computing a value concurrently. Its
exception stays hidden until you call .await() on it, so a forgotten
await() can silently swallow an error until something else surfaces it.

tips.title: delay() suspends without blocking the underlying thread
tips.content:
Thread.sleep() blocks the entire thread, preventing it from doing any
other work — on Android's main thread, this freezes the UI.

delay() is a suspend function that pauses only the coroutine, freeing the
thread to run other coroutines in the meantime. It's the coroutine-world
equivalent of sleep(), but non-blocking by design.

tips.title: SupervisorJob isolates failures in sibling coroutines
tips.content:
A regular Job cancels all siblings when one child fails. SupervisorJob
changes that — a failure in one child does not cancel the others.

This is commonly used at the root of a ViewModel's CoroutineScope so
one failed background task doesn't tear down unrelated ongoing work.

Note that supervisorScope only isolates failures one level down — if you
nest a regular coroutineScope inside, normal cancellation propagation resumes
within that nested scope.

tips.title: Use structured concurrency
tips.content:
Every coroutine should be launched in a specific CoroutineScope. 
This ensures that when the scope is cancelled (e.g., a ViewModel is cleared), 
all child coroutines are cancelled too — no leaks.

Never use GlobalScope in production. It lives for the entire app lifetime 
and makes it impossible to cancel work when it's no longer needed.

Use viewModelScope, lifecycleScope, or create your own with SupervisorJob().

tips.title: async/await for parallel work
tips.content:
Use async to run multiple tasks in parallel and await their results.
Without async, suspending calls run sequentially — one after another.

async returns a Deferred<T> which is like a Promise. 
Call .await() to get the result when you need it.

This can dramatically speed up operations that are independent of each other, 
like fetching data from two different API endpoints simultaneously.

tips.title: SupervisorJob prevents cascading failure
tips.content:
With a regular Job, if one child coroutine fails, all siblings are cancelled too.
SupervisorJob changes this: each child fails independently.

This is critical for UI work. If one network request fails, 
you don't want it to cancel other unrelated requests in the same scope.

viewModelScope already uses SupervisorJob internally, 
but if you create custom scopes, remember to use it.
